Where each of the 28 plan funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil at about $115, a yen close to the level that has triggered intervention, bond yields above 5% and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.

Update · Fri 6 Nov 2026, 9 am Manila (covers 5 Nov)
AI meltdown: Nasdaq −5.5% into correction, chip stocks −12% in a day

The post-election rally reversed sharply on 5 Nov. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% and closed in correction territory (more than 10% below its 6 Oct record). The S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,354, about 6% below its record. The chip index lost 12.3% and NVIDIA about 9%. Analysts cited worries that the new Democratic Congress will slow and raise the cost of AI data-centre building, rising electricity costs, and hedge funds locking in 2026 gains. Volatility (VIX) jumped 70% to 28. Treasuries rallied. The Bank of England raised rates to 4%. This is the AI-crash pattern the report describes; no fund rating changes, since the AI-heavy funds were already rated High or Very high.

What it means
Chip and AI stocks crashed.

Chip index (SOX) −12.3% to 9,011, NVIDIA −9.3%, AMD about −15%, Micron about −12%, Tesla −10.8%, Meta −4%. Data-centre names (IREN, Applied Digital, Nebius) fell more than 14%. The Nasdaq-100 lost about 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion of value. In Asia, Korea's KOSPI fell 5.3% (trading curbs triggered), with Samsung −7.6% and SK Hynix −9.5%. Japan's Advantest fell 14.7%, and the Nikkei broke below 60,000 this morning.
The funds rated most AI-exposed are taking the biggest hits, as the report expected. HSBC Islamic (13), Schroder Asian Opportunities (24) and Robeco EM (22) likely fell sharply over 5–6 Nov.
The broad market fell too:
S&P 500 −4.4% to 7,354, Dow −3.4% (−1,833 points), Russell 2000 −4.5%. Retail investors sold the most US stock since March 2020. Some analysts called it "capitulation" for data-centre beneficiaries.
The S&P 500 has now crossed the report's −5% level (~7,430); the −10% level is ~7,040, about 4% lower. See "Buying in a sell-off".
Shelters held.
The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.84%, lifting bond funds. Asia outside chips rose on 5 Nov: Hang Seng +3.6%, Australia's ASX +2.6%, India +2%.
Low-AI and bond funds are doing their job. Pacific (7) gained on 5 Nov but may give some back today after the US fall.
Bank of England raised rates to 4.00%
(8–1 vote; one member wanted more), its first hike since 2023. It expects UK inflation to reach 5% by mid-2027. Governor Bailey said it shouldn't be seen as the start of a long series of hikes.
Expected; a cautious tone. Neutral for the UK fund.
Oil steadied
after the previous day's 8.7% plunge: WTI +0.8% to $91.28, Brent near $98. Iran reported more tankers hit in Hormuz, and a US–Iran deal is still unconfirmed. Gold was little changed near $4,096.
No change. Oil still swings on each Iran headline.
Coming up (Manila):
US jobs report tonight 9:30 pm; US October CPI 10 Nov; NVIDIA results in late November; Fed 8–9 Dec.
NVIDIA's results are now the key test of whether the AI sell-off deepens or stabilises.

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus the plan's own processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit
An AI crash is one way to lose money; these are the others. Several are already moving markets this month. Numbers link to each fund's analysis.

1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. Japan had already spent ¥11.7 trillion defending the yen in April–May. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill at $115 a barrel. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. Iran says the strait could reopen within 4–5 days if the US lifts its blockade, but the US told non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia on 27 Oct, and talks are reportedly on hold until after the 3 Nov midterms. On 30 Oct a tanker was hit by limpet mines, the first successful such strike of the war, and Brent ended October up about 14%. Over the weekend a draft US–Iran framework was reported with Hormuz reopening within 7 days of a deal, and Iran's negotiators went to Doha. On 2 Nov Iran offered to reopen Hormuz within two days on its conditions, Trump said Iran wants a deal, and Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77. Hours later US "defensive strikes" hit Iran's Qeshm Island, and Brent steadied near $105. After the 3 Nov US election, Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62 on 4 Nov as markets priced pressure to end the war. Nothing is agreed. The strait has been largely closed since March, and October was the worst month yet for attacks on shipping. Iran says it stays shut until the US accepts its seven conditions. Houthi strikes have hit Saudi pipelines, while Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani and Qatari mediators were in Tehran this week. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%), and markets briefly priced about 50% odds of a second Fed hike this week. The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. After strong GDP and inflation data on 29 Oct, markets priced about 78% odds of a December hike, though the 10-year yield fell to 4.98% as tech sold off, and to 4.94% on 30 Oct. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002, and Pimco's CIO has said 6% is possible. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed.

5 · Taiwan tension and Asian currency stress

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out.
Hits:
Forbes
7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level, then rebounded to $3,957 on 2 Nov and $4,070 on 4 Nov. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias.

Buying in a sell-off
If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which funds in the menu tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen.
